quiz.q: What actually happens when you call an `async fn`?
options: The function body runs immediately, like a normal function
Rust returns a `Future` without running the body
Rust spawns a new OS thread to run it
The call blocks until the result is ready
quiz.explain: Calling an async fn only builds a Future — an inert state machine sitting at step zero. The body doesn't execute until something polls/awaits it.

quiz.q: An `async fn` has a `println!` as its first line. You call the function but never `.await` it. Does the `println!` run?
options: Yes, calling always runs the first line
No — calling an async fn only constructs a Future; nothing inside runs until it's driven
Only if the function has no arguments
Only in debug builds
quiz.explain: The function body is completely inert until the Future is polled by an .await or an executor. Calling it alone never executes a single line inside.

options: Anywhere in any function
Only inside an `async fn` or `async` block
Only inside `fn main`
Only inside a closure
quiz.explain: .await can only appear inside async code, because only that code has been rewritten by the compiler into a pollable state machine that knows how to pause and resume.

quiz.q: What compile error do you get from writing `value.await` inside a plain (non-async) `fn main()`?
options: E0502 — cannot borrow as mutable
E0308 — mismatched types
E0728 — `await` is only allowed inside `async` functions and blocks
No error — it's just a warning
quiz.explain: The compiler rejects .await outside async code with error E0728, since only async functions and blocks are compiled to support pausing and resuming.

quiz.q: What's the key behavioral difference between `.await` (waiting on I/O) and a blocking call like `std::thread::sleep`?
options: There's no real difference — both freeze the thread the same way
`.await` yields control back so other work can run on the same thread while waiting; `std::thread::sleep` freezes the whole thread
`.await` always runs on a different CPU core automatically
`std::thread::sleep` is always faster
quiz.explain: When a future awaited via .await isn't ready, it returns control to the executor instead of the CPU sitting idle — other work can proceed. A real blocking call has no such courtesy.

quiz.q: What does Rust's standard library provide for async, and what is it missing?
options: It provides both the async/.await syntax and a built-in executor
It provides the async/.await syntax and the Future trait, but ships no executor
It provides an executor, but no async/.await syntax
It provides neither — both come from an external crate
quiz.explain: async/.await and the Future trait are language/std features. Actually running a future to completion needs an executor/runtime, which Rust deliberately doesn't ship — you pick one, like Tokio.

quiz.q: You call an async fn but never `.await` or spawn the resulting value. What does the compiler tell you?
options: `unused implementer of \`Future\` that must be used`
`unreachable code`
`this function is deprecated`
Nothing — no warning is produced
quiz.explain: The compiler's must_use lint on Future fires with 'unused implementer of Future that must be used', noting that futures do nothing unless you .await or poll them.

quiz.q: Why doesn't wrapping a purely CPU-bound loop (no I/O waiting at all) in `async` make it faster?
options: Async always makes every program slower, period
Async's benefit comes from yielding control during I/O waits; with nothing to wait on, there's no gap to fill and only bookkeeping overhead is added
CPU-bound code cannot legally be written inside an async fn
async fn only works for functions that use the network
quiz.explain: Async concurrency comes from overlapping waiting time. A tight computation with no waiting gains nothing from being async and just carries the state-machine overhead.

flashcards.front: What does calling an `async fn` return?
flashcards.back: A `Future` — an inert value representing the work to be done. The function body has not run yet; nothing happens until the future is polled.
Drives a future forward by polling it. While it's waiting on something, it yields control back to whatever is running it instead of blocking the thread.
Only inside `async` code — an `async fn` body or an `async` block. Using it elsewhere is a compile error (E0728).

flashcards.front: What does Rust's standard library provide for async, and what does it deliberately NOT provide?
flashcards.back: It provides the `async`/`.await` syntax and the `Future` trait. It does NOT provide an executor — you need a runtime like Tokio to actually drive a future to completion.

flashcards.front: What warning appears if you create a Future and never `.await` or spawn it?
flashcards.back: `unused implementer of \`Future\` that must be used` — futures do nothing unless you `.await` or poll them.

flashcards.front: How does `.await` differ from `std::thread::sleep` while both are 'waiting'?
flashcards.back: `.await` yields the thread so other work can run while waiting; `std::thread::sleep` blocks the entire OS thread, so nothing else on it can run in the meantime.

flashcards.front: Roughly what does the compiler turn an `async fn`'s body into?
flashcards.back: A state machine implementing the `Future` trait, with a `poll` method that returns `Poll::Ready(value)` once done or `Poll::Pending` when it needs to wait.

flashcards.front: Why is async not automatically a speed boost for CPU-bound work?
flashcards.back: Async's win comes from yielding during I/O waits. A pure computation has nothing to yield during, so async adds overhead with no benefit — plain threads (or nothing) are usually better there.
